title: Backend performance review — machine-readable review
description: The machine-readable form of one review. The Markdown report (templates/review-report.md) stays the primary human artifact; this is emitted alongside it, never instead of it. Everything here must be derivable from the report — if the two disagree, the report is wrong, because a number that appears only in the JSON has escaped human review.

schema_version.description: Version of this schema the document claims to conform to. Changing a field name here is a breaking change to the project — see CHANGELOG.md.

verdict.description: Change-scoped mode only. UNKNOWN is load-bearing and must never be collapsed into PASS: it means the review could not establish whether the change regresses performance, which is different from establishing that it does not.

reproducibility.description: Everything needed to re-run this review and expect the same answer. A finding produced under one methodology version is not necessarily reproducible under another.

spec.description: The skill's frontmatter `spec` value, e.g. backend-performance-review/2.0.

detector_version.description: Version of detect_stack.py, where it was used. Absent means detection was manual.

model.description: The agent and model that produced the review. Required for any cross-model comparison to mean anything.

diff_base.description: Change-scoped mode: what the change was reviewed against.

services.description: Service topology for a monorepo, from detect_stack.py's services[]. A single-service repository may omit this. Findings scope to a service through location.service.

workload.description: The workload model the findings are scored against. Unanswered is a legitimate state — the review proceeds and caps workload-dependent findings at Medium confidence.

scenarios.description: Which operating conditions the findings were considered under. A finding can be irrelevant at normal load and severe on a cold cache.

runtime_evidence.description: Runtime artifacts supplied by the user. An empty list is why most findings cap below Confirmed, and saying so plainly is part of an honest review.

completeness.description: How much of the system this review actually saw. Without it, a reader can mistake "no findings" for "everything is healthy" — the failure mode that makes a zero-finding result dangerous instead of honest.

review_confidence.description: Confidence in the review as a whole. Distinct from any finding's confidence: every finding can be High while the review is Low, if most of the system was never examined.

repository_coverage.description: Share of in-scope code actually examined, where it can be stated honestly. Omit rather than estimate.

technology_support.description: Registry tier per detected technology, so reduced depth is visible rather than silent.

detection_confidence.description: From detect_stack.py, where it was used.

unknowns.description: What this review could not determine, and why. The two reasons are genuinely different: no evidence existing is a gap the user can close, while an unsupported technology is a gap in this skill.

assumptions.description: The assumption ledger. Separating what is known from what is assumed is what lets a reader disagree with a specific step rather than with the conclusion as a whole.

derived.description: Conclusions computed from other entries. Each states its inputs, per Hard Rule 1.

measured.description: Values that came from a real measurement. Empty is the common and honest case for a static review.

decision_changing_questions.description: Unanswered questions whose answers would change the ranking, most valuable first. More useful to a reader than "more information is needed".

root_causes.description: Underlying constraints. Several findings may share one; that is the point. A report of three symptoms under one root cause is one problem, not three.

findings.description: May be empty. Zero findings is a valid, successful result, and manufacturing findings to fill this array is the failure this project exists to prevent.

improvements.description: Performance problems this change removes or reduces. Change-scoped reviews must credit these rather than re-flagging a pattern that appears only in the diff's removed lines — reading the direction of a change before scoring it is the difference between a useful check and one teams route around.

remaining_concern.description: Required in spirit for partially-resolved: what the change did not fix.

policy_violations.description: Breaches of a policy the repository declares for itself (.performance-policy.yml). Deliberately NOT findings, and never scored on the performance rubric: a policy violation is a fact about a rule the team chose, while a finding is a claim about performance backed by evidence. Conflating them lets an arbitrary threshold inflate a severity, and lets a team's own limit masquerade as a measurement.

status.description: `not-evaluable` is the honest answer for a budget expressed against a baseline nobody measured — silently treating it as met would be a fabrication.

considered_not_reported.description: Candidates examined and discarded, with the reason. Evidence that the review had a filter — and the honest home for "theoretically inefficient, not worth optimizing".

adjacent_findings.description: Real issues found with the same evidence discipline that are not performance questions. Never scored on the performance rubric — no Severity, no Priority, no PERF- id — because those axes measure performance impact and would misrepresent a security issue as safe to deprioritize.

risk.description: A plain-language judgment with one sentence of justification — deliberately not a CVSS-style score, which this skill has no methodology to produce honestly.

assessed_properly_by.description: What dedicated review or tool would actually assess this. Pointing at the right tool is honest; pretending to be it is not.
